summary: This article profiles Friedrich Hayek, the Austrian-British economist and philosopher best known for his defence of classical liberalism. It covers his career at the London School of Economics, the University of Chicago and the University of Freiburg, his business-cycle theory and exchanges with John Maynard Keynes, and his political works such as The Road to Serfdom and The Constitution of Liberty. It also notes his 1974 Nobel Prize, his later honours, and his lasting influence.
one_line: Biography and intellectual overview of Friedrich Hayek, Austrian-British economist and philosopher known for business-cycle theory and classical liberal political thought.
key_facts: Friedrich Hayek was born on 8 May 1899 in Austria-Hungary as Friedrich August von Hayek and died on 23 March 1992 in Freiburg, Germany.
Hayek shared the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Gunnar Myrdal for pioneering work in the theory of money and economic fluctuations.
Lionel Robbins invited Hayek to join the faculty of the London School of Economics, which Hayek did in 1931.
In 1931 Hayek published Prices and Production, arguing that the business cycle resulted from central bank inflationary credit expansion and artificially low interest rates.
The Road to Serfdom was written between 1940 and 1943 and was first published in Britain by Routledge in March 1944.
Reader's Digest published an abridged version of The Road to Serfdom in April 1945 at the arrangement of editor Max Eastman.
Hayek completed The Constitution of Liberty in May 1959, and it was published in February 1960.
In 1950 Hayek left the London School of Economics for the University of Chicago, where he became a professor in the Committee on Social Thought.

From 1962 until his retirement in 1968 Hayek was a professor at the University of Freiburg, West Germany, where he began work on Law, Legislation and Liberty, published in three volumes in 1973, 1976 and 1979.
In 1984 Queen Elizabeth II appointed Hayek a member of the Order of the Companions of Honour (CH) on the advice of Margaret Thatcher, for his services to the study of economics.
In 1991 US President George H. W. Bush awarded Hayek the Presidential Medal of Freedom for a lifetime of looking beyond the horizon.
In 2011 Hayek's article The Use of Knowledge in Society was selected as one of the top 20 articles published in the American Economic Review during its first 100 years.
In February 1975 Margaret Thatcher was elected leader of the British Conservative Party, and during a 1975 meeting she held up Hayek's The Constitution of Liberty and said 'This is what we believe'.
Hayek was a second cousin on his mother's side of the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein and was one of the first to read Wittgenstein's Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus when it was published in 1921.
Milton Friedman taught Hayek's paper 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) in his graduate seminars.

entities.name: Friedrich Hayek
entities.role: Austrian and British economist and philosopher best known for his defense of classical liberalism; the article's subject

entities.name: John Maynard Keynes
entities.role: economist whose Treatise on Money Hayek critiqued in 1931 and with whom Hayek had a public exchange of letters in The Times

entities.name: Lionel Robbins
entities.role: head of the London School of Economics from 1929 who invited Hayek to join its faculty and co-signed a letter with Hayek in The Times

entities.name: London School of Economics
entities.role: institution Hayek joined as faculty in 1931 and left in 1950 for the University of Chicago

entities.name: University of Chicago
entities.role: institution where Hayek became a professor in the Committee on Social Thought in 1950

entities.name: University of Freiburg
entities.role: West German university where Hayek was a professor from 1962 until his retirement in 1968

entities.name: Milton Friedman
entities.role: economist who taught Hayek's paper 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' in his graduate seminars and was influenced by The Road to Serfdom

entities.name: Margaret Thatcher
entities.role: British Conservative leader elected in February 1975 who cited Hayek's The Constitution of Liberty and recommended Hayek for the Companions of Honour

entities.name: The Road to Serfdom
entities.role: Hayek's 1944 book on the dangers of central planning, first published by Routledge in Britain and later by the University of Chicago in the United States

entities.name: The Constitution of Liberty
entities.role: Hayek's 1960 book on liberal order, which Thatcher held up as a statement of Conservative belief

entities.name: Prices and Production
entities.role: Hayek's 1931 book, based on his LSE lectures, setting out his business-cycle theory

entities.name: Law, Legislation and Liberty
entities.role: three-volume work by Hayek published in 1973, 1976 and 1979, begun while he was at the University of Freiburg

entities.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
entities.role: philosopher and Hayek's second cousin on his mother's side, whose Tractatus Hayek read early

entities.name: Karl Popper
entities.role: philosopher of science and long-standing friend of Hayek, to whom Hayek dedicated a collection of papers

entities.name: Carl Menger
entities.role: economist whose work was Hayek's greatest intellectual debt

entities.name: Ludwig von Mises
entities.role: economist who hired Hayek as a specialist for the Austrian government and whose seminars Hayek attended

entities.name: Gunnar Myrdal
entities.role: economist who shared the 1974 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences with Hayek

entities.name: George H. W. Bush
entities.role: US president who awarded Hayek the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1991

entities.name: Nicholas Kaldor
entities.role: economist who wrote that Hayek's theory of the time-structure of capital initially fascinated the academic world

entities.name: Austrian Institute for Business Cycle Research
entities.role: institute founded and directed by Hayek in the late 1920s with the help of Mises
